title: A safety oversight system can stretch evaluation intervals as the technology it covers expands
source_unit: GAO-26-107726, Flight Simulators: FAA Should Take Steps to Ensure Oversight Efforts Address Increased Workload
geography: United States; FAA National Simulator Program oversight of flight simulators used by airlines and flight schools

observations.period: 1990–2025 simulator inventory; evaluation activity 2019–2024; report September 2026

denominator.unit: selected flight-simulator sponsors interviewed; they owned or operated over 62% of all simulators

workload.value: simulators increased by more than 500% while National Simulator Program staff remained steady
workload.unit: FAA oversight workload and staffing trend

evaluation_activity.value: number and type of evaluations remained relatively steady from 2019 through 2024

evaluation_interval.value: Extended Evaluation Interval program permits 12-month intervals to extend up to 36 months for qualifying simulators

communication.value: 6 of 10 selected sponsors raised concerns about communication; 2 cited potential safety issues from longer intervals

skills.value: FAA identified staffing and mission-critical skills gaps, including standards development, but had not addressed all of them

recommendations.unit: open recommendations to improve sponsor feedback and address mission-critical skills gaps

observations.method: GAO reviewed FAA policies, guidance, data, laws, regulations, evaluation activity, and workforce-planning material; interviewed FAA officials and a nongeneralizable sample of 10 sponsors; and conducted two site visits to a simulator manufacturer and flight-training organization.
observations.uncertainty: The sponsor sample is not generalizable, though it covers over 62% of simulators. The report does not estimate accident risk, simulator-specific error, pilot performance, or the causal effect of longer evaluation intervals. Stable evaluation counts can reflect an effective risk-based program, workload constraints, or both. Simulator oversight is one part of aviation safety and does not represent all FAA safety functions.
observations.subgroup: Major and regional airlines, flight schools, simulator and aircraft manufacturers, and FAA National Simulator Program staff; simulator technologies and operator types differ.
observations.counterinterpretation: Extending evaluation intervals for consistently high-performing simulators may be an efficient risk-based strategy rather than a safety reduction. Sponsor concerns may reflect communication gaps without proving unsafe determinations. Steady staff can become more productive through improved processes, and the report does not quantify uncompleted evaluations.

related_sources.claim: Official GAO report PDF provides the workload trend, evaluation intervals, sponsor interviews, skills gaps, and recommendations.

boundary: This record adds a physical-safety infrastructure layer: oversight coverage can be maintained through risk-based interval extensions while workload, communication, and specialist skills remain under pressure. It does not establish unsafe simulators, pilot error, accident risk, or a causal effect of evaluation intervals on aviation safety.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GAO landing page and full report PDF; FAA simulator inventory and sponsor records are not retained.
